question: How does an HTTP request work?
note: Two agents, one question. The control was forbidden to read skill/SKILL.md, so its voice is untouched. The PSTE arm read the standard and also ran the checker on itself.
control:
Alright, at a high level: your browser or code needs to send a request to a server, and that starts with figuring out where the server actually is. If you typed a domain name, DNS resolves that to an IP address first — that's its own little lookup chain (browser cache, OS cache, resolver, root/TLD/authoritative servers) but the end result is just an IP.

Once you've got the IP, a TCP connection gets established with the server (the three-way handshake: SYN, SYN-ACK, ACK) on whatever port, usually 443 for HTTPS or 80 for HTTP. If it's HTTPS there's also a TLS handshake layered on top before any actual data moves — that's where certs get exchanged and verified, and a symmetric key gets negotiated for encrypting everything after.

Then the actual HTTP request goes out over that connection. It's just text (even in HTTP/2 and /3 it's conceptually the same, just framed differently) — a method like GET or POST, a path, headers (host, content-type, auth tokens, cookies, whatever), and optionally a body if you're sending data.

The server receives it, and whatever's on the other end — nginx, an app server, a load balancer, whatever — parses it, routes it to the right handler, does whatever logic it needs to do (hit a database, call another service, whatever), and builds a response. The response comes back with a status code (200, 404, 500, etc.), its own headers, and usually a body with the actual content, often JSON for an API or HTML for a page.

Your client reads that response, and depending on what it is, does something with it — renders a page, parses JSON, throws an error if the status code says something went wrong, etc.

The connection either gets closed or, more commonly these days, kept alive and reused for subsequent requests so you're not paying the TCP/TLS setup cost every single time.
pste:
A browser sends a request. A server sends back a response. The request has three parts: a method, a URL, and headers.

The method names the action. `GET` reads data. `POST` sends new data. The URL names the resource on the server. The headers give extra facts, such as the content type or an authentication token.

The browser opens a TCP connection to the server first. It then sends the request over that connection. DNS turns the domain name into an IP address before the connection opens.

The server reads the request. It runs the matching code. It builds a response and sends it back on the same connection.

The response has a status code, headers, and a body. The status code names the result.

`200` means success. `404` means the server did not find the resource. `500` means the server failed while it built the response. The body holds the data itself: HTML, JSON, or another format.

HTTPS adds one step. The browser and the server agree on an encryption key before they send the request. This stops a third party from reading the data on the network.

The whole exchange is stateless. The server does not remember the last request from the same browser. An app that needs memory across requests stores a session ID in a cookie, and the browser sends that cookie back with each new request.

I did not cover WebSockets or HTTP/2 multiplexing here. Ask if you need those.
